subject: physics

items.q: Which statement best describes the colours of the visible light spectrum?
items.correct: Each colour covers its own narrow band of wavelength and frequency
items.misconception: Each colour is one exact wavelength paired with one exact frequency
items.why: Spectrum diagrams in books print a single value next to each colour, and questions often quote 'red light of wavelength 700 nm', which makes each colour look like one fixed number. Read the specification wording literally: each colour has a narrow band of wavelength and frequency. The bands sit next to each other and run continuously into one another, which is why the spectrum has no gaps or sharp lines in it.
items.random_wrong: Each colour has its own wavelength band but they share a frequency

items.q: Red light is at one end of the visible spectrum and violet light at the other. Which comparison is correct?
items.correct: Red light has a longer wavelength and a lower frequency than violet
items.misconception: Red light has a longer wavelength and a higher frequency than violet
items.why: Red is associated with heat and danger, and infrared sits next to red in the spectrum, so students assume red is the 'most energetic' end. Order the visible spectrum: red has the longest wavelength and lowest frequency, violet the shortest wavelength and highest frequency. Infrared lies beyond red precisely because it has an even longer wavelength and even lower frequency.
items.random_wrong: Red light has the same frequency band as violet but is longer in wavelength

items.q: A beam of parallel light rays hits a sheet of white paper and leaves in many different directions. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: Diffuse reflection: the rough surface reflects the rays in many directions
items.misconception: Diffuse reflection: the law of reflection does not hold at a rough surface
items.why: The scattered rays clearly are not parallel, and students conclude that the rule they learned for mirrors has been abandoned rather than applied point by point. Draw the normal at several points on a bumpy surface. Each normal points a different way, so identical incoming rays meet different surfaces and leave in different directions — every one of them still obeying the law of reflection.
items.random_wrong: Absorption: a rough surface takes light in instead of reflecting it back

items.q: A wall painted with matt paint shows diffuse reflection. Which statement about the individual rays is correct?
items.correct: Each ray still obeys the law of reflection, but the normals point different ways
items.misconception: The law of reflection is broken, because the rays leave at completely random angles
items.why: The scattered rays clearly are not parallel, and students conclude that the rule they learned for mirrors has been abandoned rather than applied point by point. Draw the normal at several points on a bumpy surface. Each normal points a different way, so identical incoming rays meet different surfaces and leave in different directions — every one of them still obeying the law of reflection.
items.random_wrong: Only a mirror can obey the law of reflection, so painted walls simply scatter light

items.q: You can see your face in a still pond, but not when the wind puts ripples on it. Why?
items.correct: Still water is smooth and gives specular reflection; ripples scatter the light
items.misconception: Rippled water absorbs the light, so almost none of it returns to your eyes
items.why: 'No image' is read as 'no reflection', and absorption is the only other process students can name for light that appears to have gone. White paper is bright, so it must be reflecting most of the light that reaches it. If it absorbed the light it would look black. The light is reflected, but scattered.
items.random_wrong: Only a mirror is smooth enough to reflect light well enough to form an image

items.q: How does a green colour filter work?
items.correct: It transmits green light and absorbs the other wavelengths
items.misconception: It adds green colour to whatever light passes through it
items.why: The filter looks red and the light coming out is red, so students read it as a dye or a paint being added rather than as a subtraction. Filters take away. The beam leaving a red filter is dimmer than the beam entering it, because the wavelengths that were absorbed are missing. A filter can never put a wavelength into a beam that was not there before.
items.random_wrong: It changes the wavelength of the light passing to green

items.q: White light is shone through a red filter and then through a green filter onto a screen. What is seen on the screen?
items.correct: No light, because the green filter absorbs the red light the first filter transmits
items.misconception: Red light, because once light has left the first filter its colour cannot be removed
items.why: Students treat the light as having been permanently 'set' to a colour, and forget that the second filter absorbs every wavelength except green. Apply each filter in turn to the wavelengths actually present. After the red filter only red remains; a green filter absorbs red, so nothing is transmitted and the screen stays dark.
items.random_wrong: Green light, because the second filter changes the red light passing through it

items.q: A red rose with green leaves is viewed through a blue filter in white light. How does it appear?
items.correct: Both the petals and the leaves appear black
items.misconception: The petals appear blue and the leaves appear blue
items.why: The filter looks red and the light coming out is red, so students read it as a dye or a paint being added rather than as a subtraction. Filters take away. The beam leaving a red filter is dimmer than the beam entering it, because the wavelengths that were absorbed are missing. A filter can never put a wavelength into a beam that was not there before.
items.random_wrong: The petals appear red and the leaves appear black

items.q: What determines the colour of an opaque object seen in white light?
items.correct: The wavelengths of light that it reflects most strongly
items.misconception: The wavelengths of light that it absorbs most strongly
items.why: Students know that the colour is somehow 'taken' by the object, and absorbing feels like the active process, while reflection sounds like nothing happening. Only light that reaches your eye can be seen. The colour of an opaque object is determined by which wavelengths are more strongly reflected; the wavelengths that are not reflected are the ones absorbed.
items.random_wrong: The wavelengths of light that pass right through it

items.q: A jumper appears blue in white light. Which statement describes what the jumper is doing?
items.correct: It reflects blue light strongly and absorbs the other wavelengths
items.misconception: It absorbs blue light strongly and reflects the other wavelengths
items.why: Students know that the colour is somehow 'taken' by the object, and absorbing feels like the active process, while reflection sounds like nothing happening. Only light that reaches your eye can be seen. The colour of an opaque object is determined by which wavelengths are more strongly reflected; the wavelengths that are not reflected are the ones absorbed.
items.random_wrong: It transmits blue light and reflects all the other wavelengths

items.q: A book that looks red in white light is placed in a room lit only by green light. How does it look, and why?
items.correct: Black, because it absorbs the green light and no red light is there to reflect
items.misconception: Red, because the colour belongs to the book and the lighting cannot change it
items.why: Colour is treated as a fixed property painted onto the object, rather than as the result of which wavelengths reach the eye. The colour seen depends on the object and on the light falling on it. An object can only reflect wavelengths that are actually shone at it, so a red object in green light reflects nothing and appears black.
items.random_wrong: Green, because the book reflects back whatever light happens to be shone on it

items.q: Why does an object appear white when white light shines on it?
items.correct: Because all of the wavelengths are reflected equally
items.misconception: Because all of the wavelengths pass straight through it
items.why: 'Lets all the light through' and 'sends all the light back' both mean 'nothing is stopped', so students pick transmission when the object is opaque. An opaque white object such as a sheet of card transmits no light at all — hold it up and no light gets through. It looks white because every wavelength is reflected equally.
items.random_wrong: Because it reflects only the white wavelengths of light

items.q: A black surface is placed in a brightly lit room. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: It absorbs all wavelengths of the light falling on it
items.misconception: No light is reaching it, which is why it looks black
items.why: Darkness and black look identical, so absence of light and absorption of light get treated as the same explanation. A black car in sunlight is in bright light and still looks black, and it gets hot — evidence that the light is arriving and being absorbed rather than never arriving.
items.random_wrong: It transmits all wavelengths, so none comes back out

items.q: What is the difference between a transparent object and a translucent object?
items.correct: Both transmit light, but a translucent object scatters the light it transmits
items.misconception: Both transmit light equally well, so the two words mean the same thing
items.why: Both words are used loosely in everyday English for anything that is not solid-looking, and both really do transmit light. Test it by trying to read print through the material. Through clear glass the print is sharp (transparent); through frosted glass or tracing paper light still gets through but the print cannot be read (translucent).
items.random_wrong: A transparent object transmits light and a translucent one absorbs it

items.q: Frosted glass in a bathroom window lets light into the room, but you cannot see clearly through it. The glass is:
items.correct: translucent, because it transmits the light but scatters it
items.misconception: opaque, because no clear image can be seen through it
items.why: Students judge by whether an image is visible rather than by whether light is transmitted, and 'blocked view' becomes 'blocked light'. Ask whether the room behind the material gets any light. A frosted bathroom window is bright, so light is being transmitted; it is translucent, not opaque. An opaque object transmits no light at all.
items.random_wrong: transparent, because the light still gets through the glass

items.q: A shirt with red and white stripes is viewed in white light through a red filter. What is seen?
items.correct: All of the shirt looks red, so the stripes can no longer be told apart
items.misconception: The red stripes look red and the white stripes stay white as before
items.why: Colour is treated as a fixed property painted onto the object, rather than as the result of which wavelengths reach the eye. The colour seen depends on the object and on the light falling on it. An object can only reflect wavelengths that are actually shone at it, so a red object in green light reflects nothing and appears black.
items.random_wrong: All of the shirt looks white, because the filter adds red to the white

items.q: Light from a lamp passes through a piece of blue stained glass. Which explains why the light beyond it is blue?
items.correct: The glass transmits blue light and absorbs the other wavelengths
items.misconception: The glass turns the white light into blue light as it passes through
items.why: The words 'the light turns red' are used loosely in everyday speech, and students take 'turns' as a change happening to each wave rather than as a selection between waves. Think of a filter as a gate, not a paint pot: some wavelengths are let through unchanged and the rest are absorbed. Shine pure green light at a red filter and nothing comes out — there is nothing for it to change.
items.random_wrong: The glass absorbs blue light and transmits the other wavelengths

items.q: Do all the colours of visible light have the same frequency?
items.correct: No. Each colour has its own narrow band of frequency as well as its own narrow band of wavelength; the two change together.
items.misconception: Colours differ in wavelength, but they are all light, so they must all have the same frequency.
items.why: Students meet 'visible light travels at the same speed' and mistakenly transfer 'the same' from speed to frequency, treating wavelength as the only property that varies. For waves travelling at the same speed, wave speed = frequency × wavelength, so if the wavelength band is different the frequency band must be different too. A change in wavelength forces a change in frequency.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can any surface other than a mirror give specular reflection?
items.correct: Yes. Specular reflection is reflection from any smooth surface in a single direction — still water, polished metal and glossy paint all show it.
items.misconception: Specular reflection only happens with mirrors; everything else scatters light.
items.why: Every worked example and ray diagram in class uses a mirror, so the term becomes attached to the object rather than to the smoothness of the surface. The property that matters is how smooth the surface is compared with the wavelength of light, not what the object is called. A still pond gives specular reflection; the same pond with ripples on it gives diffuse reflection.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is white a colour of the visible light spectrum?
items.correct: No. White light is all the wavelengths of the visible spectrum together, and an object appears white because it reflects all of them equally.
items.misconception: White is its own colour with its own wavelength, so a white object reflects the white wavelengths and absorbs the rest.
items.why: White is treated like any other colour in art and in everyday speech, and paint mixing gives no clue that white light is a mixture of wavelengths. The visible spectrum runs red to violet; there is no band labelled white. A white object appears white because all wavelengths are reflected equally, and it takes on the colour of any coloured light shone on it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
